title: Category Specialists: Filling a Need
brief: Which players are strong in one category (PTS, REB, AST, ST, BLK, 3PTM) and could fill a hole late in the auction or in season? It must warn that one-category players look better in punt rankings than they are and should not be bought to fix a category already lost.
summary: A category specialist helps only when he moves a category you can still win each week. Buy him late in the auction or with a waiver move, after you know which categories are close. Punt rankings make one-category players look like top 100 players. Do not pay that price, and never buy one to rescue a category you have already lost.

paragraphs.text: When a ranking punts a one-category player's weak categories, he can look like a top 100 player. That view hides what he costs you everywhere else. Our league drafts 144 players, so a top 100 spot in a punt ranking does not mean he deserves a roster spot in our standard 9-cat format.

Watch for three common traps. First, big men who are elite only in blocks, FG% and rebounds get overdrafted. Do not take them as early as round three, which is about picks 25 to 36 in a 12-team league. Second, strong steals alone should not raise a player's value. Third, a guard who only shoots threes and gives no rebounds or assists is a bad profile unless he is elite at threes.

If you take a two-category player early, he leaves holes you then have to fill. In our auction it is worse. A big early bid on a narrow player creates the holes and also uses up the dollars you need to fill them.

sections.heading: Do not buy back a lost category

paragraphs.text: Never draft a one-category specialist to fix a category that is already too weak to recover. In head-to-head you need to win 5 of 9 categories each week. A specialist who adds a little to a category you lose by a wide margin wins you nothing. His weak categories then cost you elsewhere.

During the auction, update your category strengths and weaknesses after every buy. Before you bid on a specialist, ask one question: is this category close for my build? If you have punted it, pass. If you are already strong in it, pass too. Bid only when it is a real need, for example a big man for rebounds or a guard for assists.

Use the same test in season, before you spend FAB or one of your 6 weekly acquisitions. Look at your weekly results. If you lose a category narrowly, a specialist can swing it. If you lose it badly every week, spend the move somewhere else. Make this call well before the trade deadline on 2027-03-04, so the roster is set for playoff weeks 19 to 21.

sections.heading: When to reach: the experts differ

paragraphs.text: The experts do not agree on how hard to chase a need. One side says you sometimes have to reach, for example taking a player a bit early just to get assists, and that a reach is fine if it fits your build because you do not have to be rigid about value. The other side warns that when you are weak in a category like assists, you should not overindex on chasing it.

In practice the two views fit together. Pay a few dollars over value for a specialist when the category is close and he fits the build you are already running. Do not let one weak category take over your whole auction plan, and do not pay early-round money for it.

sections.heading: Where specialists fit in our league

paragraphs.text: Specialists belong late in the auction, once your build is clear and you know which categories are close. Early dollars should go to players who help many categories, because early narrow buys leave holes.

Look at what a specialist costs you, not just what he adds. FG% and FT% are team ratios, so a high-volume poor shooter can sink one of them. A specialist whose costs land in a category you already punt is a good fit. One whose costs land in a category you still contest is not, unless he is elite in his strong category.
